I can kind of understand what he's saying. To speak from my own experience, I am a LARPer. That is, a player of Live-Action Roleplaying Games. (If you think you've never heard of it, go watch the movie "Role Models." It's not perfect but it gets the idea across well enough.) I was a player - just a player, I paid to go to events, played a character, played NPCs when I was required to, and nothing more - for about two and a half years. When I realized I was too night-blind to play safely for half the event, and thus couldn't work as an NPC for entire events, I learned to write content for the game and joined the Plot Committee - the Game Masters, the directors, the guys who run the events - so that I could continue to give back to the community even though I could not participate by fighting as the occasional bad guy any more.

And that transition does change your perspective. You know how content comes to exist. You know the behind-the-scenes secrets. You know exactly how professional your colleagues are (and aren't). You cry into your beer over storylines that should have been awesome that people inexplicably hated, and laugh all the way to the bar over the random crap you came up with at the last possible minute that ended up being a huge hit.

I imagine being a developer is kind of like that. Is it necessary to be a gamer to develop good games? It probably helps, but it's not strictly necessary. Do you inherently get more out of one if you are also the other? Probably not; they really are two separate things. Writing/developing content and playing it are both enjoyable, but in different ways.

You won't be able to sample at that rate directly from the Arduino. The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem, simply stated, is that the you need a sampling frequency double that of the signal you are sampling. This is why the base sampling rate for CD technology is 44,100 Hz. This gives a maximum effective frequency of the signal sampled to be 22,050 Hz, or just above the typical human hearing top end. That's a very simplified version of it since there is much more to it, but it illustrates the point. With the Arduino overhead, you'd be lucky to sample at 40 KHz for audio or maybe 5 MHz for discreet square wave signals. I think to possibly achieve the sampling rate you desire at 1 GHz, you would need an FPGA or some really specialized signal processing devices. Arduino will not get you there.
